title: Fried Plantain
subtitle: Sweet ripe plantain slices fried until golden and caramelised
excerpt: The simplest and most satisfying side dish in West African cooking. Very ripe plantain fried until the sugars caramelise and the edges turn crisp. Three ingredients, perfect every time.
sourceNotes: A staple side dish across West and Central Africa, the Caribbean, and Latin America.

content.text: This serves 4 as a side and takes about 15 minutes. The thing to watch is the ripeness of the plantain: the skin must be mostly black, not yellow. A yellow plantain will not caramelise properly and tastes starchy rather than sweet.
Do not rush the cooking. Let each side sit undisturbed for 3-4 minutes until it develops a proper golden crust before turning. Moving them too early means they stick and the caramel layer tears.

items.prepNote: peeled and cut on the diagonal into 1cm slices

content.text: Peel the plantain by cutting off both ends and slitting the skin along the length. Slice diagonally about 1cm thick.
Heat the oil in a large frying pan over medium heat until shimmering.
Add the plantain slices in a single layer, not overlapping. Do not crowd the pan.
Fry undisturbed for 3-4 minutes until the underside is deep golden and caramelised.
Turn with tongs and fry the other side for 2-3 minutes until equally golden.
Drain on kitchen paper. Sprinkle with a pinch of salt if using. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: Plantain is starchy and not sweet
items.fix: Leave at room temperature for several days until the skin is mostly black before frying

items.symptom: Plantain stuck to the pan and tore when turned
items.cause: Turned before the crust formed fully
items.fix: Wait until you can see the golden edge creeping up the side before attempting to turn

items.symptom: Plantain is burnt on the outside but soft and wet inside
items.fix: Keep heat at medium and take the extra time - they need 3-4 minutes per side to cook through

content.text: Fried ripe plantain is eaten throughout West Africa, Central Africa, the Caribbean, and much of Latin America wherever the plantain grows. In Nigeria it is called dodo and served alongside jollof rice at parties and celebrations. In Cote d'Ivoire it is called alloco. The same dish appears under different names from Accra to Havana, always made the same way: very ripe, simply fried, and eaten immediately.
